7750: Hike has two completely separate, unrelated meanings depending on the context. A third, specialized meaning exists in American football. Here is each one explained fully.
Meaning 1 — A Long Walk in Nature

A hike is a long walk taken outdoors, on natural terrain such as mountains, forests, hills, valleys, or countryside trails.

What makes a hike different from a regular walk?

A walk is casual and can happen anywhere — on a street, in a mall, around a park. A hike is different in three key ways:

  • It happens in a natural, outdoor setting (not in a city or on paved roads).
  • It is physically more demanding — it involves climbing, uneven ground, or long distances.
  • It usually takes a significant amount of time, often hours.

People go on hikes for enjoyment, fitness, adventure, or to experience nature.

Examples in sentences:

  • "We went on a hike through the mountains."
  • "The hike to the waterfall was beautiful but tiring."
  • "It's a three-hour hike to the top."

Common descriptive phrases:

  • A short hike vs. a long hike — refers to distance or time.
  • A tough hike vs. an easy hike — refers to physical difficulty.
  • A scenic hike — a hike with beautiful views along the way.
  • A day hike — a hike completed within a single day, without camping overnight.
Meaning 2 — A Significant Increase (in price, rate, or cost)

This meaning is very commonly found in news, economics, and everyday conversations about money.

A hike here means a noticeable, sharp increase — usually in something financial, such as prices, taxes, wages, interest rates, or fees.

Key nuance: The word "hike" is not used for tiny, barely-noticeable increases. It signals a change that is large enough to be felt and noticed. It often carries a slightly negative tone — the people affected by the increase usually did not welcome it.

Examples in sentences:

  • "There has been a hike in fuel prices." → Fuel became more expensive.
  • "The government announced a tax hike." → Taxes went up significantly.
  • "The workers demanded a pay hike." → They wanted a notable raise in salary.
  • "The bank approved an interest rate hike." → Borrowing money became more expensive.

Very common fixed combinations (you will hear these constantly):

  • Price hike — an increase in the cost of goods or services.
  • Tax hike — an increase in taxes people must pay.
  • Rate hike — an increase in interest rates (used heavily in banking and economics).
  • Pay hike / Wage hike — an increase in salary or hourly wages.
  • Fare hike — an increase in the price of public transport (bus, train, etc.).
  • Rent hike — an increase in how much someone pays to live somewhere.

This meaning is narrow and only applies to the sport of American football.

A hike is the act of the center (a specific player on the team) snapping — that is, passing the ball backward between their legs — to the quarterback to officially start a play. The word is also used as a command: "Hike!" means "start the play now."

You only need this meaning if you watch or discuss American football.
How to Always Know Which Meaning Is Intended

Since the two main meanings are completely unrelated, the surrounding words in a sentence will always make it obvious:

  • If the sentence is about nature, walking, trails, or outdoors → it is Meaning 1.
  • If the sentence is about money, prices, taxes, rates, or wages → it is Meaning 2.
  • If the sentence is about American football → it is Meaning 3.

There is never any real ambiguity in practice.

"Hike" as a noun always contains the idea of something going up — either your body moving up and through nature on a long walk, or a number rising sharply. That mental image of "upward movement" is a useful thread connecting both major meanings.
7751:
Meaning 1: To walk a long distance, especially in nature

This is the most common meaning. When you hike, you walk a long distance — usually through mountains, forests, hills, or countryside. It is not just any walk. It carries the sense of physical effort, distance, and being in an outdoor, natural setting.

Examples:

  • "We hiked through the forest for six hours."
  • "She hiked along the river trail every weekend."
  • "They hiked ten miles before setting up camp."

What separates hiking from ordinary walking:

  • The terrain is usually uneven, steep, or rough — not a flat city pavement.
  • It takes much longer — usually hours.
  • It involves noticeable physical effort.
  • It happens in nature, and often for recreation or adventure.

You can also say "go hiking" (this is equally common):

  • "Let's go hiking this Sunday."
  • "Have you ever gone hiking in the mountains?"

Both mean the same thing — the only difference is phrasing.
Meaning 2: To raise or increase something sharply

In this sense, "hike" means to increase a price, rate, tax, salary, or fee — usually by a large amount, and often suddenly or unexpectedly. This meaning is very common in news, business, and economic conversation.

Examples:

  • "The government hiked fuel prices by 20%."
  • "The central bank hiked interest rates to slow down inflation."
  • "The landlord hiked the rent without warning."
  • "Airlines hiked ticket prices during the holiday season."

Important nuance — tone: Saying someone "hiked" a price sounds more alarming and dramatic than saying they "raised" or "increased" it. The word "hike" quietly suggests that the increase is steep, unwelcome, or abrupt. Journalists and writers use it precisely for this reason — it adds a sense of urgency or criticism.

So: "The company raised its prices" feels neutral. "The company hiked its prices" sounds sharper — almost like a complaint.

What can be "hiked" in this sense: Almost always something measurable — prices, fares, fees, taxes, interest rates, wages, costs. You would not use "hike" for vague or abstract things.
Meaning 3: To pull something upward sharply

This meaning is more physical and everyday. When you "hike" something, you grab it and pull it up firmly and quickly — usually a piece of clothing that has slipped down or needs to be raised.

This meaning almost always appears as the phrasal verb "hike up", not "hike" alone.

Examples:

  • "She hiked up her skirt to cross the muddy stream."
  • "He hiked up his trousers before kneeling on the floor."
  • "The child hiked up his socks."

The image is of a quick, firm yank upward — not a slow, gentle lift.
The Phrasal Verb "Hike Up" — Used for Both Meaning 2 and Meaning 3

You will notice that "hike up" works for both:

  • "They hiked up the prices." → raised the prices (Meaning 2)
  • "She hiked up her sleeve." → pulled her sleeve up (Meaning 3)

The context makes it clear which meaning is intended. If it is followed by clothing, it means to pull up. If it is followed by a price, cost, rate, or fee, it means to raise.
Register and Tone — When Is Each Meaning Used?

Nature/walking sense: Used in both casual and formal speech. Universally common.

Price/rate sense: Very common in journalism, economics, and business conversation. Carries a slightly negative, dramatic tone — implying the increase was large or unwelcome. Not used for small, expected increases.

Pull-up sense: Casual and informal, mostly in everyday spoken or written language.
The Three Meanings at a Glance

1. Walk long distances in nature → "They hiked the mountain trail."
  2. Raise prices/rates sharply → "The bank hiked interest rates."
  3. Pull clothing upward → "He hiked up his trousers."
7752:
Hilarious means extremely funny — so funny that it makes you laugh hard, loudly, or even uncontrollably. It is not just "a little funny" or "mildly amusing." It is the kind of funny that makes you burst out laughing, maybe even struggle to breathe or hold your stomach.

Think of it as sitting on a scale of funniness:

Amusing → Funny → Very funny → Hilarious → Side-splitting

"Amusing" is when something makes you smile gently. "Funny" is when you chuckle. "Hilarious" is when you laugh so hard you can't stop — it sits near the top of that scale.

Almost anything that makes people laugh intensely can be described as hilarious:

  • A joke — "He told a hilarious joke at the party."
  • A movie or TV show — "That comedy film was absolutely hilarious."
  • A situation — "It was a hilarious moment when the dog stole the wedding cake."
  • A person — "She is hilarious — everything she says makes me laugh."
  • A story or anecdote — "He shared a hilarious story about getting lost in Tokyo."
  • A video or post — "That meme is hilarious!"
  • Something unexpected or absurd — "The look on his face was hilarious."

When you call a person hilarious, you mean they are naturally and consistently very funny — they have a gift for making people laugh.
How intense is the laughter it describes?

The laughter "hilarious" points to is not polite or soft. It is loud, real, and often hard to control. You might:

  • laugh until your eyes water
  • slap your knee
  • double over
  • struggle to speak because you're laughing so much

If something is merely funny, people chuckle. If something is hilarious, people lose it.
How it is used in everyday speech

Hilarious is very common in casual, everyday English. People use it freely — sometimes even slightly exaggerated — to express that something was really, really funny.

Common patterns you will hear:

  • "That was hilarious!" (after something funny happens)
  • "I find him absolutely hilarious."
  • "We were laughing at the most hilarious thing."
  • "You have to watch this — it's hilarious."

Common words paired with it (collocations):

  • absolutely hilarious — the most common pairing; adds emphasis
  • utterly hilarious — same meaning, slightly more formal
  • genuinely hilarious — stresses that it is truly funny, not just a polite compliment
  • pretty hilarious — softer; means quite funny
  • find something hilarious — "I found the whole situation hilarious."

Sometimes "hilarious" is used sarcastically — meaning the opposite of what it literally says. The tone of voice (or context in writing) makes this clear.

For example, if someone plays an annoying prank on you and you say, "Oh, hilarious," with a flat or cold tone, you actually mean: "That was not funny at all."

This sarcastic use is common in real-life conversation and informal writing. Context always tells you which meaning is intended.
How it differs from similar words

WordWhat it meansIntensity of laughter
AmusingMildly entertaining; makes you smileA gentle smile
FunnyGeneral term for something that causes laughterA chuckle
ComicalFunny in a silly, clownish, or visual wayA laugh
HumorousHas a quality of humor; gentler, more thoughtfulA soft laugh or smile
HilariousExtremely funny; causes hard, uncontrollable laughterLoud, intense laughter
  • Amusing is gentle. A mildly entertaining story is amusing, not hilarious.
  • Funny is the everyday, middle-ground word. Most things that make you laugh are "funny."
  • Comical usually describes something visually silly — like a person falling in a clumsy way, or a ridiculous costume.
  • Humorous has a more intelligent, refined feel — a clever essay can be humorous even if it never makes you laugh loudly.
  • Hilarious is the strongest of these in terms of the intensity of laughter it describes.

• Hilariously (adverb) — describes how something is done in a funny way.
    "The cat hilariously knocked the glass off the table."
    "His speech was hilariously bad."
  • Hilarity (noun) — the state or quality of being very funny; the laughter and fun that results.
    "The room erupted in hilarity."
    "Much hilarity followed when the clown tripped."

Hilarious = extremely funny; causes intense, hard-to-control laughter.

It is stronger than "funny." It describes jokes, situations, people, videos, or stories that make people laugh loudly and fully. It is used freely in casual conversation, sometimes with slight exaggeration, and occasionally sarcastically to mean the opposite.
7753: Hilarity means a state of great, often loud and uncontrollable laughter and amusement — usually shared among a group of people. It is not just "being happy" or "finding something a little funny." It is the peak of amusement. Think of that moment at a dinner table where someone says something so funny that everyone bursts out laughing at the same time and can barely stop — that collective explosion of laughter is hilarity.

There are two slightly different ways this word is used, and both are correct:

1. Hilarity as a state people are in.
This is when a group of people are in a state of great laughter and amusement.

"The comedian's joke sent the whole room into hilarity."

Here, hilarity is the state the audience entered — they were all laughing loudly together.

2. Hilarity as a quality that something has.
This is when you use the word to describe how funny a situation, event, or thing is.

"The hilarity of the situation was impossible to ignore."

Here, hilarity means the extreme funniness of a situation.

Both uses point to the same idea: something at a very high level of funny.

Understanding what kind of funny "hilarity" points to is important. Not all laughter is hilarity. Here are its key qualities:

  • It is intense. A polite chuckle is not hilarity. Hilarity involves deep, hearty, often breathless laughter.
  • It is often shared. Hilarity is almost always a group experience. While one person alone can find something hilarious, the word "hilarity" most naturally describes a moment where a group of people are all laughing together.
  • It is often spontaneous. Hilarity frequently bursts out suddenly — triggered by something unexpected, absurd, or that went hilariously wrong.
  • It is warm, not cruel. Hilarity generally carries a positive, joyful energy. It is not the laughter of mockery or spite. It is pure, fun amusement.

One of the most common situations where the word "hilarity" is used is when something goes unexpectedly wrong in a funny, harmless way. For example:

"The groom forgot his vows and started making them up on the spot, much to the hilarity of the guests."

This is a classic hilarity moment — something went off-script in a funny way, and everyone laughed.

In fact, the phrase "much hilarity ensued" is extremely common in English. It is used — often humorously — to describe a funny chain of events that followed something.

"He tried to parallel park in front of the crowd. Much hilarity ensued."
Degree: Where Does It Sit on the Scale?

Think of amusement on a scale:

Mild smile → Chuckle → Laughter → Hilarity

Hilarity sits right at the top. It is the strongest form of shared, loud amusement. This is why something described as causing "hilarity" is considered very funny — not just mildly entertaining.
Common Ways It Appears in Sentences

The word "hilarity" most often appears in a few reliable patterns. Getting familiar with these will help you use and recognise it naturally:

  • "erupted into hilarity" — the group suddenly started laughing loudly.
  • "dissolved into hilarity" — the group gradually broke down into laughter, losing composure.
  • "much to the hilarity of [someone]" — something happened that made a particular group laugh a lot.
  • "the hilarity of the situation" — referring to how funny a situation was.
  • "cause/provoke hilarity" — something triggered great laughter.
  • "ensue in hilarity / hilarity ensued" — laughter and amusement followed.

It helps to draw clear lines:

  • Not just happiness. You can be happy without laughing. Hilarity is specifically about laughter and amusement.
  • Not just a smile. Hilarity implies something far stronger than a quiet smile.
  • Not sarcasm or dark humour. Hilarity is warm and light. Words like "cynicism" or "dark comedy" occupy a different space.
  • Not individual. While one person can find something hilarious, hilarity as a noun most naturally describes a shared, communal moment of laughter.

These words are related to hilarity but differ in small, important ways:

  • Amusement — milder than hilarity; you can be amused without laughing out loud.
  • Merriment — joyful and fun, but broader; merriment includes singing, dancing, and celebration, not just laughter.
  • Glee — a feeling of delight and joy, often with a slightly childlike or triumphant quality; less specifically about laughter than hilarity.
  • Mirth — a more formal or literary word for cheerful laughter and joy; very close in meaning to hilarity, but used in more old-fashioned or poetic writing.

Of all these, mirth is the closest synonym to hilarity.

If you ever want to quickly recall what hilarity means, remember this image:

A room full of people laughing so hard they can barely breathe, some holding their stomachs, some wiping tears from their eyes — that is hilarity.
Hilarity is a noun that means a state of great, loud, and often contagious shared laughter and amusement — the highest, most infectious form of finding something funny.
7754:
A hillock is a small hill — a gentle, rounded rise of land that is noticeably higher than the ground around it, but clearly too small and modest to be called a proper hill or a mountain.

Think of it as a bump in the landscape. Not dramatic, not steep, not towering — just a soft, low mound of earth rising quietly from the surrounding ground.
Size and scale — where it fits

To understand a hillock well, it helps to place it on a scale:

Flat ground → hillock → hill → mountain

A hillock sits right at the bottom of that scale, just above flat terrain. There is no strict measurement — nature doesn't come with labels — but in general, a hillock could be anywhere from a few feet to perhaps a couple of hundred feet tall. What matters more than exact height is the feel of it: it is small, low, and unimposing. You could easily walk up one without effort.

A hill is noticeably larger and more prominent. A mountain is vast and dramatic. A hillock is neither — it is gentle, humble, and easy to overlook.

Hillocks are almost always rounded and smooth on top — like the back of a sleeping animal half-buried in the ground. The slopes are gradual, not sharp or jagged. This rounded, soft quality is central to the word. If you picture it, it looks like the land is taking a slow, easy breath upward.

A hillock can be either natural or artificial.

Natural hillocks are formed over long periods by the earth itself — through the shifting of soil, deposits left behind by glaciers, erosion carving away the land around a harder core, and so on. You'll find them scattered across fields, meadows, moorlands, and open countryside.

Man-made hillocks are created by human hands, deliberately or as a byproduct of activity. Ancient peoples, for example, built hillocks as burial mounds — piling earth over the graves of the dead. Over centuries, these settle and grow over with grass, looking almost natural. Hillocks can also form when rubble, earth, or debris accumulates in one spot over time.
How it differs from similar words

English has several words for small rises in the ground, and they overlap quite a bit. Here's how hillock sits among them:

  • Knoll — nearly the same as hillock. A small, rounded, grassy hill. The two are often used interchangeably. Knoll has a slightly more poetic feel.
  • Mound — a pile of earth, which could be natural or man-made. A mound can be smaller and more deliberately shaped than a hillock, and the word is often used when talking about constructed piles of dirt.
  • Hummock — a small, lumpy rise, often found in wetlands, marshes, or frozen ground. It tends to suggest something more irregular or uneven than a hillock.
  • Rise — a very gentle, broad increase in elevation. A rise is often flatter and less distinct than a hillock.

Among all these, hillock is the most general and straightforward word for a small, rounded hill in an open landscape.

Hillock is used most often in:

  • Written descriptions of landscapes — geography, travel writing, nature essays
  • Literature and poetry, especially older English writing — novelists and poets describing the English countryside, rural Ireland, the Scottish moors, ancient battlefields
  • Historical and archaeological writing — when describing burial mounds, earthworks, or ancient land formations

It is a somewhat formal or literary word. In everyday casual speech, most people would just say "a little hill" or "a small mound." But in writing — especially descriptive writing — hillock is precise and evocative. It tells the reader exactly the right size, shape, and mood of the landform.

• The shepherd sat on the grassy hillock, watching the flock below.
  • A lone tree grew from the top of a small hillock at the edge of the field.
  • Archaeologists discovered that what looked like a natural hillock was in fact an ancient burial mound.
  • Children ran up and rolled down the hillock, laughing in the afternoon sun.
  • From the hillock, one could see the entire village spread out in the valley.

Beyond its literal meaning, hillock carries a certain gentle, peaceful quality. It doesn't suggest danger or grandeur. When a writer uses hillock, they are usually painting a quiet, pastoral scene — open countryside, soft light, a modest rise in the land. It belongs to the vocabulary of calm, rural landscapes.

A hillock is a small, gently rounded hill or mound — larger than a simple bump in the ground, but far too modest to be called a proper hill, found naturally in open landscapes or built by human hands, and most at home in calm, rural settings.
7755:
A hilt is the handle of a sword, dagger, or knife — the part that you hold in your hand when using the weapon.

Think of a sword as being made of two main parts: the long, sharp blade, and the hilt — everything that makes up the handle end. The hilt is what separates your hand from the dangerous part.
What a Hilt Is Made Of

A hilt is not just one simple piece. It is actually a small assembly of parts working together:

1. The Grip
This is the central part of the hilt — the section you literally wrap your fingers around. It is often made of wood, leather, bone, or wrapped cord to give a firm, comfortable hold.

2. The Guard (or Crossguard)
This is a piece that sits between the grip and the blade, often shaped like a horizontal bar or a disc. Its job is purely protective — it stops an enemy's blade from sliding down onto your hand during a fight. It also stops your own hand from accidentally slipping forward onto your own blade.

3. The Pommel
This is the knob or weighted cap at the very bottom end of the hilt (the end furthest from the blade). It acts as a counterbalance to the weight of the blade, making the sword easier to control. It also prevents the hand from slipping off the bottom of the grip.

So to summarise: grip + guard + pommel = hilt.

• She grabbed the sword by the hilt and pulled it from its scabbard.
  • The hilt was decorated with gold and precious stones, though the blade itself was plain steel.
  • He gripped the dagger's hilt tightly as he crept forward.

This is where the word goes beyond swords and enters everyday language. The phrase "to the hilt" means completely, fully, or to the absolute maximum degree.

The image behind it is vivid: if you thrust a sword into something all the way up to the hilt, there is nothing left to push — the blade has gone in as far as it possibly can. The hilt is the stopping point.

So "to the hilt" means pushed to the very limit — nothing held back.

Examples:

  • He was in debt to the hilt. (He owed as much money as he possibly could — completely swamped in debt.)
  • She supported her team to the hilt. (She backed them completely and without any reservation.)
  • The company exploited every loophole to the hilt. (They used every loophole to the absolute maximum.)
  • He was mortgaged to the hilt. (He had borrowed as much as the bank would possibly allow against his home.)

You'll notice this phrase always carries the sense of no room left, nothing more possible — the absolute limit has been reached.
A Quick Way to Remember It

A hilt is to a sword what a steering wheel and dashboard are to a car — the control end, the part built for the human hand, designed for grip, safety, and balance.

And "to the hilt" = all the way. Completely. 100%.

You'll come across hilt most often in:

  • Descriptions of historical weapons, armour, and warfare
  • Fantasy novels, films, and games involving swords (think medieval settings)
  • The phrase "to the hilt" in journalism, business writing, and everyday conversation — this is the form you'll likely see most in modern life
7756:
To hinder someone or something means to make it harder for them to do something, move forward, or make progress. It puts obstacles, difficulty, or delay in the way — but it does not necessarily mean stopping something completely.

Think of it this way: imagine you are trying to walk forward, and someone keeps slowing you down by pulling lightly on your backpack. They are not stopping you entirely. You are still moving, but with great difficulty. That pulling force? That is what "hinder" captures.

The most important thing to understand about this word is where it sits on a scale:

Easy → Difficult → Hindered → Blocked/Prevented → Completely Stopped

"Hinder" lives in the middle. It is about creating friction and difficulty — not a full wall, but a serious slowdown. This is what makes it different from words like "prevent" or "stop," which suggest something is completely blocked. When something is hindered, there is still a chance of moving forward, but it is much harder.

"Hinder" is a transitive verb, which means it always acts on something — it always has an object. You hinder something or someone.

Two main patterns:

Pattern 1: hinder + noun/pronoun

"The storm hindered the rescue operation."
"His injury hindered him."

Pattern 2: hinder + someone + from + verb(-ing)

"Her lack of confidence hindered her from speaking up."
"The noise hindered them from concentrating."

Seeing a word in many different contexts is the best way to truly own it. Here is "hinder" across several real-life situations:

Physical situations:

  • "The thick mud hindered the soldiers' march through the forest." (The mud didn't stop them, but made every step a struggle.)
  • "Poor visibility hindered the pilot's ability to land safely."

Work and progress:

  • "A lack of proper tools hindered the construction team."
  • "Constant meetings hindered her from finishing the report on time."

Learning and growth:

  • "His unwillingness to ask questions hindered his learning."
  • "Anxiety can seriously hinder a student's performance in exams."

Relationships and communication:

  • "The language barrier hindered communication between the two teams."
  • "Mistrust hindered the peace negotiations."

Health:

  • "The pain in his knee hindered his ability to exercise regularly."

Notice that in every single example, the "hindering" thing is creating difficulty and slowing progress — but not always completely shutting it down.

Since learners often confuse nearby words, it is important to draw clear lines:

  • Hinder ≠ Stop/Prevent. "Stop" or "prevent" means something is fully blocked. "Hinder" means it is made harder or slower. "The rain prevented the match" (no match at all). "The rain hindered the match" (the match happened, but with great difficulty).
  • Hinder ≠ Help/Facilitate. These are direct opposites. To "facilitate" means to make something easier. To "hinder" means to make it harder.
  • Hinder ≠ Destroy. Hindering does not mean ruining something entirely. It means creating obstacles along the way.

When you use the word "hinder," you are pointing to something that acts like dead weight on progress — a force that drags, slows, or gets in the way. The hindrance could be:

  • A person (a rival, a bad manager, a noisy neighbour)
  • A thing (weather, poor equipment, a missing document)
  • An internal quality (fear, self-doubt, laziness, stubbornness)
  • A situation or condition (poverty, illness, conflict, bureaucracy)

Any of these can hinder progress, goals, movement, or people.

Since you are learning comprehensively, here are the word's other forms so you recognize them in the wild:

  • Hindered (past tense): "The bad weather hindered the team yesterday."
  • Hindering (present participle): "Stop hindering my work!"
  • Hindrance (noun): "His attitude was a hindrance to the group's success." (A hindrance is the thing that hinders — the obstacle itself.)
  • Unhindered (adjective/adverb): "She moved through the crowd unhindered." (Meaning: freely, without any obstacle.)
To hinder = to make progress, movement, or action harder, slower, or more difficult — like an obstacle that weighs you down without necessarily stopping you completely.
7757:
Hindmost means furthest to the back — the one positioned at the very rear of a group, line, or series, behind everyone or everything else.

Think of a line of people queuing outside a shop. The very last person standing at the tail end of that line — the one with the most people in front of them — is the hindmost person.

It answers the question: "Who or what is the most behind?"

The word "hind" on its own already means "at the back" or "rear" — you may have heard it in phrases like "hind legs" (the back legs of an animal). "Hindmost" takes that idea and pushes it to its furthest extreme: not just at the back, but the furthest back of all.

It works just like other superlatives:

  • Small → smallest (the most small)
  • Far → farthest (the most far)
  • Hind → hindmost (the most toward the back)

So "hindmost" always implies a comparison. You can only call something hindmost when there are others ahead of it. It is the last of a group, the tail end, the very bottom of a sequence.

Physical position:

  • The hindmost soldier in the march was struggling to keep up.
    (The soldier at the very back, behind all the others.)
  • She chose the hindmost seat in the cinema so no one would sit behind her.
    (The seat furthest to the rear of the hall.)
  • The hindmost carriage of the train was the quietest.
    (The last carriage, at the tail of the train.)

Abstract / figurative use:

  • Safety was the hindmost thought in his reckless mind.
    (Safety was the very last thing he was thinking about — pushed furthest to the back of his concerns.)
  • The new recruits found themselves hindmost in priority when resources were handed out.
    (They were given the least attention, treated as the last in importance.)
An Important Nuance: Position vs. Sequence

"Hindmost" can describe either physical position (who or what is at the back in space) or order/priority (who or what comes last in importance, time, or rank).

Both uses share the same core idea: pushed to the furthest extreme of "behind."
The Famous Phrase: "Devil Take the Hindmost"

This is a well-known expression in English that directly uses this word, and understanding it will cement the meaning for you.

"Devil take the hindmost" means: every person should look after themselves, and whoever is the slowest or the last will suffer the consequences.

It paints the picture of people fleeing in panic. Everyone rushes ahead to save themselves. The devil, chasing from behind, will catch whoever is last — the hindmost person. The message is blunt: don't be last, or you'll pay the price.

This phrase is used today to describe ruthlessly competitive or self-serving behaviour, where nobody helps those who fall behind.
Register and Tone: When Is This Word Used?

"Hindmost" is a formal and somewhat literary word. In everyday conversation, most people would simply say "last," "at the back," or "rearmost." You are more likely to encounter "hindmost" in:

  • Formal writing
  • Literature, especially older texts
  • Fixed expressions like "devil take the hindmost"
  • Military or ceremonial descriptions

It carries a slightly old-fashioned, dignified feel. Using it in casual speech would sound unusually elevated — not wrong, but noticeable.
How It Differs from Similar Words

ConceptWordShade of meaning
  • Last — the most general, everyday word. Can mean last in time, order, or position.
  • Rearmost — very close to "hindmost"; means furthest to the rear. Slightly more technical or spatial.
  • Hindmost — specifically emphasises being furthest behind in a group, with a slightly formal, literary tone. Works for both space and priority.

The distinction is subtle. In most situations, "hindmost" and "rearmost" are interchangeable. The difference is mainly in feel: "rearmost" sounds clinical, while "hindmost" sounds more classical.
Quick Summary to Lock It In

Hindmost = the one that is furthest behind of all — the last, the rearmost, whether in a physical line, a sequence, or a list of priorities. It is a formal, somewhat old-fashioned adjective most famously used in the phrase "devil take the hindmost," which warns that those who fall behind face the worst consequences.
7758:
A hindrance is anything — a person, a thing, a situation, or even an internal quality like a habit or a feeling — that makes something harder to do, slows you down, or gets in the way of your progress toward a goal.

The soul of this word is: it holds you back.

A hindrance does not always stop you completely. It makes the path harder — it creates friction, delay, or extra effort. Think of it like trying to run with a heavy backpack. You can still run, but the backpack slows you down, drains your energy, and makes the whole effort harder. That backpack is a hindrance.

This is what separates "hindrance" from something like a "blockade," which implies a total stop. A hindrance hampers you. It complicates things. But you can still push through it — just with greater difficulty.

Almost anything can be a hindrance, which is part of what makes this word so useful. It is not limited to physical things.

A person:
"His constant interruptions were a hindrance to the team's focus."

A physical thing:
"The heavy snow was a hindrance to the rescue operation."

A situation or circumstance:
"Poverty can be a hindrance to getting a good education."

A personal quality or feeling:
"Shyness can be a hindrance in job interviews."

A system or process:
"Excessive paperwork can be a hindrance to efficiency."

This wide range is important. A hindrance lives wherever something is being slowed down, complicated, or made harder — regardless of whether the cause is physical, emotional, or abstract.

"Hindrance" behaves in two ways:

As a countable noun (you can say a hindrance or hindrances):
"Lack of sleep is a hindrance to clear thinking."
"There are several hindrances the team needs to overcome."

As an uncountable noun (used in a general sense, without an article):
"The supplies arrived without hindrance."
"She worked without hindrance all morning."

"A hindrance to [something]" — This is the most natural and common structure. The word "to" links the hindrance to whatever it is making harder.
"Fear of failure can be a hindrance to taking risks."
"Office politics can be a hindrance to real progress."

"More of a hindrance than a help" — A very widely used phrase meaning something causes more problems than it solves, even if it was supposed to help.
"His constant advice during the project was more of a hindrance than a help."

"Without hindrance" — Meaning freely, with nothing standing in the way.
"The convoy passed through without hindrance."

"Prove to be a hindrance" — When something turns out to get in the way, often unexpectedly.
"His perfectionism proved to be a hindrance when the deadline was tight."

"Hindrance" is a moderately formal word. It sits comfortably in essays, formal emails, newspaper articles, and educated everyday conversation. It is not slang, not overly technical, and not cold or clinical. It simply sounds like the language of a thoughtful, educated person.
How It Compares to Similar Words

Getting this right will sharpen your understanding considerably.

Obstacle — Tends to be more concrete and specific — something you must get around or over. It can imply a complete block. "The fallen tree was an obstacle on the road." An obstacle is often something you can point to.

Barrier — Carries a stronger sense of a wall or firm dividing line that firmly prevents passage. "A language barrier." "A trade barrier." It feels more structural and absolute than a hindrance.

Impediment — Almost interchangeable with hindrance in many contexts, and slightly more formal. However, "impediment" is especially fixed in certain specific usages, most notably a speech impediment (a condition that makes speaking difficult) and legal language ("without let or impediment").

Hindrance — Specifically stresses the idea of hampering, complicating, and slowing down. It carries a sense of friction built into it. Where "barrier" feels like a wall, "hindrance" feels like mud — you can get through it, but it makes everything harder.

1. "She admitted that procrastination was her greatest hindrance to success."
  2. "The language difference was a significant hindrance during the negotiations."
  3. "Heavy traffic is a daily hindrance for millions of commuters."
  4. "Overregulation can act as a hindrance to innovation in the tech industry."
  5. "Despite every hindrance thrown at them, the team delivered on time."
  6. "His lack of confidence was more of a hindrance than his lack of experience."
  7. "The aid workers managed to reach the affected villages without hindrance."
If you had to remember just one thing: a hindrance is anything that makes progress harder — not necessarily impossible, but noticeably more difficult, slower, or more complicated.
7759:
Hindsight is the ability to look back at something that already happened and understand it clearly — often more clearly than you did when it was actually happening.

Think of it this way: when you are in the middle of a situation, you cannot see the full picture. You don't know how things will turn out. But once it is all over, and you can look back at it, everything suddenly makes much more sense. That clear understanding you gain afterwards — that is hindsight.

In the simplest possible terms: hindsight = understanding something better because you are looking at it from the past.
Why Does This Word Even Exist?

Because humans have a very interesting quality: we often understand things better after they happen than while they are happening. This is so common and so universal that the English language gave it its own word.

When you are making a decision, you are working with limited information. You don't know the future. But once the event is over, you now have extra knowledge — you know exactly what happened and why. Looking back with that extra knowledge gives you a clearer picture. That retrospective (backward-looking) clarity is what "hindsight" captures.

You will almost always see this word used in the phrases "in hindsight" or "with hindsight." These phrases mean: "Now that I/we know how things turned out, looking back at it..."

Think of "in hindsight" as a door you walk through before saying what you now understand about a past event.

Examples:

  • "In hindsight, I should have studied harder for the exam."
    → At the time, you thought you had studied enough. Now that you've failed, you understand you hadn't.
  • "With hindsight, the warning signs were obvious."
    → While the problem was developing, no one noticed. But now, looking back, the signs are clear.
  • "In hindsight, investing all the money in one company was a mistake."
    → The person thought it was a good idea at the time. The outcome revealed otherwise.

You will very often hear the expression "Hindsight is 20/20." This is one of the most commonly used phrases in English, and it uses "hindsight" at its core.

"20/20" refers to perfect vision — it means you can see with perfect clarity. So the expression means: when you look back at the past, your understanding is always perfectly clear, because you already know exactly what happened.

In other words, it is easy to judge past decisions and say "I should have done this" or "that was obviously a mistake" — but only because you already know the result. At the time of the decision, things were not so clear.

This phrase is often used to defend a decision that turned out badly, or to remind someone not to judge a past decision too harshly. For example:

  • "Sure, we can see it was a bad plan now — but hindsight is 20/20. We didn't know it would fail."
What Hindsight Is Not — Important Distinctions

To truly understand a word, it helps to see what it is not. There are two closely related words you should know:

Foresight is the opposite of hindsight. Foresight is the ability to think ahead and understand what might happen before it happens. If hindsight is looking backwards with clarity, foresight is looking forward with wisdom.

  • "She had the foresight to save money before the crisis hit."

Insight sits in the middle. Insight means a deep understanding of something — but it is not tied to before or after. You can have insight during an event, before it, or after it. Insight is about depth of understanding, not timing.

TimingMeaning
ForesightBefore an eventUnderstanding what might happen
InsightAnytimeA deep understanding of something
HindsightAfter an eventUnderstanding what did happen, in retrospect
The Deeper Psychological Layer: Hindsight Bias

Here is something important that will deepen your understanding of this word significantly.

Psychologists have identified something called hindsight bias, and it is directly connected to the concept of hindsight. Hindsight bias is the very human tendency to look back at a past event and believe that you knew it was going to happen all along — even when you didn't.

After a team loses a match, people say, "I knew they were going to lose!" After a business fails, people say, "It was obvious that would happen." But in reality, they did not know. The outcome felt predictable only because they already knew it.

Hindsight bias is sometimes called the "I-knew-it-all-along" effect. It distorts memory and makes people overconfident — because the past, viewed through hindsight, always seems more predictable than it actually was.

This is why hindsight is a double-edged concept:

  • On one hand, it genuinely helps you learn from the past.
  • On the other hand, it can trick you into thinking you were wiser than you were.

Hindsight appears constantly in real life, in all kinds of situations:

  • Personal decisions: "In hindsight, I shouldn't have quit that job."
  • Relationships: "With hindsight, I can see we were just incompatible."
  • History: "In hindsight, the Great Depression had many warning signs that were ignored."
  • Health: "In hindsight, those symptoms were early signs of the illness."
  • Sports: "In hindsight, the coach's decision to change tactics in the second half was a mistake."

Hindsight is the understanding or judgment of a past event that comes after it has happened — clearer and sharper than it ever could have been in the moment, because now you know exactly how things turned out.
